text: Anant Maral Shastri (1912–1999) was an Indian freedom fighter, journalist, literary figure, poet, Sanskrit scholar, linguist, and administrator. He left Ambikapur, now in Chhattisgarh, at a young age to join Kashi Vidyapeeth in Varanasi, where he studied under Acharya Narendra Dev and Acharya JB Kriplani, both prominent freedom fighters. His grandfather, Pandit Lal Bihari Sharma, was the official tutor of Raja Bahadur Raghunath Saran Singh Deo, Maharaja of Sarguja (1879–1917), who was the great-grandfather of Madaneswar Saran Singh Deo, who later became Chief Secretary of Madhya Pradesh. Pandit Lal Bihari Sharma owned a large landed property in Ambikapur, Sarguja, which his only son and heir, Anant Maral, left behind when he joined Kashi Vidyapeeth and the freedom movement at a young age and never returned to claim it after Independence. During the Civil Disobedience Movement (1930–1932), when the British suppressed the press, Anant Maral went underground, published the Congress Bulletin and Congress Samachar from Allahabad, wrote the texts by hand, cut stencils to print copies, and distributed them by foot across villages to spread the Congress message. He also served as Youth League secretary in Varanasi. After earning the Shastri degree, he moved to Lahore, where he briefly worked as a college professor before becoming editor of Hindi Milap, a prominent newspaper, gaining significant popularity in literary circles. In 1945, he published a well-researched treatise on the Bhakti Movement titled "Ram Bhakti Shakha" in Lahore (now in Pakistan), which was prescribed as a textbook for MA Hindi Literature by Punjab University during the pre-Independence period, with a preface written by renowned Hindi scholar and former All India Radio director Udayshankar Bhatt. In 1942, during the Quit India Movement, he was arrested and imprisoned at Patna Camp Jail, where Sitaram Kesri, later Congress President, was also a cellmate. Upon Independence, he moved from Lahore to Delhi and joined the Publications Division of the Government of India as editor of Ajkal, the highest-circulated and most popular Hindi magazine of the time, which became a platform for many emerging poets. At the Publications Division, he played a key role in compiling and editing Mahatma Gandhi's Prayer Speeches, recorded earlier by All India Radio, which were later published as "Bhaiyon aur Behnon" (Brothers and Sisters). In 1949, Anant Maral Shastri was appointed Director of Information and Publicity in Madhya Bharat, a position he continued in Madhya Pradesh after the state reorganisation in 1956, serving until 1971. During his tenure, the Tansen Samaroh in Gwalior (a music festival commemorating Miyan Tansen, one of Akbar’s nine gems) and the Kalidas Samaroh in Ujjain (a festival honoring the great Classical Sanskrit poet and dramatist Kalidas) reached their peak of glory. India’s first President, Dr. Rajendra Prasad, inaugurated the first Akhil Bharatiya Kalidas Samaroh (National Kalidas Festival) in 1958, with Prime Minister Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru as chief guest at the second, during which Nehru was presented with Kalidasa’s famous work, Raghuvansh, translated from Sanskrit to Hindi by Anant Maral Shastri. This initiative was taken by BV Keskar, Union Minister for Information and Broadcasting (1952–1962), who transformed the Tansen Samaroh into a national music festival. For nearly two decades, Anant Maral also led the Madhya Pradesh Shasan Sahitya Parishad and Kala Parishad (State Councils for Literature and Arts). Major events such as the Tagore Centenary, Alauddin Khan Centenary, and the 1960s celebration at Khandwa honoring the legendary Hindi poet Makhanlal Chaturvedi were highlights that brought immense pride to Madhya Pradesh.
